q: Electric current can be classified as two types: direct current (DC) and alternating current (AC).
e: True. DC keeps one direction, the steady flow you get from a battery. Be classified as two types: direct current (DC) and alternating current (AC).

q: The direct current is a current that reverses its direction at regular time intervals.
e: False. The right claim is this: An alternating current is a current that reverses its direction at regular time intervals. Current is charge passing a point each second, and it needs a closed path. The printed line wrongly says the direct current is a current that reverses its direction at regular time intervals.

q: In a direct current the electrons flow steadily in the same direction all the time.
e: True. In metals the mobile carriers are electrons, drifting opposite the conventional-current arrow. Current the electrons flow steadily in the same direction all the time.

q: The current that flows in a flashlight, cell phones, laptops, and any appliance running on the batteries is direct current.
e: True. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. Phones, laptops, and any appliance running on the batteries is direct current.

q: An alternating current is a steady unidirectional current.
e: False. The right claim is this: The direct current is a steady unidirectional current. DC keeps one direction, the steady flow you get from a battery. The printed line wrongly says an alternating current is a steady unidirectional current.

q: In the alternating current the direction of the flow of electrons changes periodically.
e: True. AC reverses on a clock; household supply is this reversing current. In the alternating current the direction of the flow of electrons changes periodically.

q: Current flowing in power lines and normal household electricity from a wall outlet (plug) is alternating current.
e: True. Current is charge passing a point each second, and it needs a closed path. And normal household electricity from a wall outlet (plug) is alternating current.

q: In Japan and in the most of America, the voltage is between 220V and 240V.
e: False. The right claim is this: In Japan and in the most of America, the voltage is between 100 V and 120 V. Voltage is potential difference, energy per unit charge between two points. The printed line wrongly says in Japan and in the most of America, the voltage is between 220V and 240V.

q: Europe and most other countries in the world (including Myanmar) use a voltage between 220V and 240 V.
e: True. Voltage is potential difference, energy per unit charge between two points. The value 220V is the figure this statement is using.

q: The frequency of AC current is 60 Hz in Europe and most other parts of the world.
e: False. The right claim is this: The frequency of AC current is 50 Hz/60 Hz in Japan, 60 Hz in US and 50 Hz in Europe and most other parts of the world. Current is charge passing a point each second, and it needs a closed path. The printed line wrongly says the frequency of AC current is 60 Hz in Europe and most other parts of the world.

q: When a coil of wire having quite a few turns is rotated a few cycles per second continuously in a magnetic field, an emf is induced in the coil.
e: True. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. Continuously in a magnetic field, an emf is induced in the coil.

q: In each revolution the current produced in the coil due to the induced emf, rises to a maximum value, then falls to zero, reverses, rises to a maximum and falls to zero again.
e: True. A changing magnetic flux through a loop produces an induced emf and, if the path is closed, an induced current. To zero, reverses, rises to a maximum and falls to zero again.

q: The waveform of the induced emf in an AC generator is called a square wave.
e: False. The right claim is this: The waveform of the emf shown in Figure 11. 3 is called a sine wave. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop.

q: A rotating coil in a magnetic field is the basic of an AC generator.
e: True. AC reverses on a clock; household supply is this reversing current. A rotating coil in a magnetic field is the basic of an AC generator.

q: The advantage of alternating current is that it is relatively difficult to change the voltage of the current.
e: False. The right claim is this: The advantage of alternating current is that it is relatively easy to change the voltage of the current. Current is charge passing a point each second, and it needs a closed path. The printed line wrongly says the advantage of alternating current is that it is relatively difficult to change the voltage of the current.

q: The inevitable loss of energy that occurs when current is distributed over long distances is far smaller with alternating current than with direct current.
e: True. DC keeps one direction, the steady flow you get from a battery. Long distances is far smaller with alternating current than with direct current.
